In brief

The victim-to-be wraps his fiancée in his arms and addresses her, not as Sarah, but as "Sheila, my own." Sheila is an uncommon but venerable Irish name. In some poems written when the English were consolidating their hold on the country it became attached to a mythical female figure who predicts the liberation of Ireland. Several 19th century writers worked to keep this allegorical tradition alive, one of them a poetic hero of Joyce's, another one his contemporary.

At more length

Sheila is an Anglicized version of Síle (old Irish Sighile), itself possibly derived from the Latin name Celia. It may figure in the ancient stone carvings called Sheela na Gigs, and an old tradition holds that either the wife or mother of Saint Patrick was named Sheila. Until the time of the Great Hunger in the mid-19th century, the Irish used to celebrate Sheelah's Day (Lá 'le Síle) on March 18, just after the saint's day. Liberal consumption of alcohol began on the day before Saint Patrick's and continued for three days. The 1856 painting reproduced here, titled "The 16th, 17, and 18th March," shows the festival in full swing.

But the usage most relevant to Joyce is probably the Irish-language genre of the aisling (ASH-ling). These poems were first composed in the early 17th century or the late 16th, when the plantation policy was strengthening English rule over Ireland. They gained fresh impetus after William of Orange defeated the Catholic King James. During the Protestant Ascendancy of the 1790s and 18th century, hopes for a Jacobite uprising were nourished by ballads in which Ireland appears personified in much the same manner as the Shan Van Vocht: either as a haggard old woman or as one who is young and beautiful. The woman in these visions tells the poet that his subjugated country will throw off its chains. Sometimes she is called Síle Ní Ghadhra (Shiela ní Gara, Sheela na Guire, Sheila na Geira).

James Clarence Mangan, whom Joyce admired extravagantly, translated an 18th century Irish poem with this title in 1849. A similar poem with the same title was translated by John D'Alton in 1831. It is reasonable to suppose that Joyce knew Mangan's translation, and at least one more example of the form was produced at the end of the century by the journalist and poet Anna Bella Johnston (1864-1902), aka Mrs. Seumas MacManus, aka Ethna Carbery, who worked with Alice Milligan on the nationalist monthly The Shan Van Vocht. Inspired by the Gaelic Revival, Carbery wrote an original English-language poem titled Shiela ni Gara. Her Shiela predicts "joy sadly won," after "the flash and crash of battle." 

In the final line of the poem Carbery calls Shiela the "Dark Rose of our Passion." Like the Róisín Dubh (Dark Rose) inspired by an actual O'Neill of that name, the many lyrics about Sheila masked revolutionary hopes under the guise of love songs. This practice perfectly accounts for Joyce's revolutionary hero-martyr addressing his beloved as "Sheila, my own." He is speaking allegorically of his hopes for a liberated Ireland, as Irish poets had been doing for centuries.

John Hunt 2026
